events.text:
## Answer

**Britannica (1771–1797)** describes Erfurt in a single short entry, headword "ERFURT" [B:2473:9]:

> "ERFURT, a large and beautiful city of Upper Saxony in Germany, capital of Thuringia, and subject to the elector of Mentz; E. long. 11° 7′, N. lat. 51° 0′."

The raw OCR of this entry is garbled — it reads "capital of **Thailand**, and subject to the **elckor of Menus**; E. long.117 é′, N.lax. 910" — but I checked the page scan and the true reading is "capital of **Thuringia**, and subject to the **elector of Mentz**" (Mentz being the old English name for Mainz), with coordinates 11° 7′ E, 51° 0′ N [B:2473:9, scan: page row 2473]. The match to Wikipedia is confirmed (status: matched, not uncertain; rerank logit −5.81, margin 1.51) [B:2473:9].

**Wikipedia** (article "Erfurt", revision 1352872890) [W:9481:1352872890] describes Erfurt as:

> "Erfurt … is the capital and largest city of the Central German state of Thuringia, with a population of around 216,000. It lies in the wide valley of the River Gera, in the southern part of the Thuringian Basin, north of the Thuringian Forest."

Wikipedia adds that Erfurt's old town is one of the best preserved medieval centres in Germany, with the Merchants' Bridge (Krämerbrücke), Erfurt Cathedral (housing the world's largest free-swinging medieval bell), St Severus' Church, and Petersberg Citadel [W:9481:1352872890]. It notes Erfurt was first mentioned in 742 when Saint Boniface founded the diocese, that it was a Hanseatic League member, part of the Electorate of Mainz in the Holy Roman Empire, part of Prussia from 1802, and part of East Germany from 1949 to 1990 [W:9481:1352872890].

## Comparison

- **Agreement**: Both call Erfurt a capital city in Germany — Britannica: "capital of Thuringia … subject to the elector of Mentz" [B:2473:9]; Wikipedia: "capital … of Thuringia … part of the Electorate of Mainz during the Holy Roman Empire" [W:9481:1352872890]. (Britannica's OCR output misreads "Thuringia" as "Thailand" and "elector of Mentz" as "elckor of Menus"; the scan confirms the correct words.)
- **Knowledge change**: Britannica gives coordinates (E. long. 11° 7′, N. lat. 51° 0′) and a qualitative judgment ("large and beautiful"); Wikipedia gives modern geography (River Gera valley, Thuringian Basin), population (~216,000), and 20th-century political history (Prussia 1802, GDR 1949–1990) that Britannica, written before those events, cannot cover [B:2473:9] [W:9481:1352872890].

**Inference**: The two sources agree on Erfurt's identity and its historic tie to the Electorate of Mainz/Mentz; the apparent disagreement ("capital of Thailand") is an OCR error, not a factual difference. The real drift is coverage: Britannica's entry is a one-sentence gazetteer description, while Wikipedia adds modern geography, demographics, landmarks, and full political history.

**Evidence**: [B:2473:9] (Britannica entry ERFURT, incl. page scan correcting the OCR); [W:9481:1352872890] (Wikipedia article Erfurt, rev. 1352872890).

On the Erfurt Cathedral Hill is the ensemble of Erfurt Cathedral —which houses the world's largest free-swinging medieval bell —and St Severus' Church. Petersberg Citadel is one of the largest and best preserved town fortresses in Central Europe. Erfurt's Old Synagogue is the oldest synagogue in Europe, and together with the Erfurt Mikveh, which was only rediscovered in 2007, and the Stone House, forms the UNESCO World Heritage Site Jewish-Medieval Heritage of Erfurt.

The city's economy is based on agriculture, horticulture and microelectronics. Its central location has made it a logistics hub for Germany and central Europe. Erfurt hosts the second-largest trade fair in eastern Germany (after Leipzig), as well as the public television children's channel KiKa. The city is on the Via Regia, a medieval trade and pilgrims' road network. Erfurt Main Station is the junction of the Nuremberg–Erfurt and the Erfurt–Leipzig/Halle high-speed lines with the Halle–Bebra railway.

Erfurt was first mentioned in 742, as Saint Boniface founded the diocese. Although the town did not belong to any of the Thuringian states politically, it quickly became the economic centre of the region and was a member of the Hanseatic League. It was part of the Electorate of Mainz during the Holy Roman Empire, and became part of the Kingdom of Prussia in 1802. From 1949 until 1990 Erfurt was part of the German Democratic Republic (East Germany).

The University of Erfurt was founded in 1379, making it the first university to be established within the geographic area which constitutes modern Germany. It closed in 1816 and was re-established in 1994. Martin Luther (1483–1546) was its most famous student, studying there from 1501 before entering St Augustine's Monastery in 1505. Other noted Erfurters include the medieval philosopher and mystic Meister Eckhart (c. 1260–1328), the Baroque composer Johann Pachelbel (1653–1706) and the sociologist Max Weber (1864–1920).

## Answer

**Britannica (1771–1797)** describes Erfurt in a single short entry, headword "ERFURT" [B:2473:9]:

> "ERFURT, a large and beautiful city of Upper Saxony in Germany, capital of Thuringia, and subject to the elector of Mentz; E. long. 11° 7′, N. lat. 51° 0′."

The raw OCR of this entry is garbled — it reads "capital of **Thailand**, and subject to the **elckor of Menus**; E. long.117 é′, N.lax. 910" — but I checked the page scan and the true reading is "capital of **Thuringia**, and subject to the **elector of Mentz**" (Mentz being the old English name for Mainz), with coordinates 11° 7′ E, 51° 0′ N [B:2473:9, scan: page row 2473]. The match to Wikipedia is confirmed (status: matched, not uncertain; rerank logit −5.81, margin 1.51) [B:2473:9].

**Wikipedia** (article "Erfurt", revision 1352872890) [W:9481:1352872890] describes Erfurt as:

> "Erfurt … is the capital and largest city of the Central German state of Thuringia, with a population of around 216,000. It lies in the wide valley of the River Gera, in the southern part of the Thuringian Basin, north of the Thuringian Forest."

Wikipedia adds that Erfurt's old town is one of the best preserved medieval centres in Germany, with the Merchants' Bridge (Krämerbrücke), Erfurt Cathedral (housing the world's largest free-swinging medieval bell), St Severus' Church, and Petersberg Citadel [W:9481:1352872890]. It notes Erfurt was first mentioned in 742 when Saint Boniface founded the diocese, that it was a Hanseatic League member, part of the Electorate of Mainz in the Holy Roman Empire, part of Prussia from 1802, and part of East Germany from 1949 to 1990 [W:9481:1352872890].

## Comparison

- **Agreement**: Both call Erfurt a capital city in Germany — Britannica: "capital of Thuringia … subject to the elector of Mentz" [B:2473:9]; Wikipedia: "capital … of Thuringia … part of the Electorate of Mainz during the Holy Roman Empire" [W:9481:1352872890]. (Britannica's OCR output misreads "Thuringia" as "Thailand" and "elector of Mentz" as "elckor of Menus"; the scan confirms the correct words.)
- **Knowledge change**: Britannica gives coordinates (E. long. 11° 7′, N. lat. 51° 0′) and a qualitative judgment ("large and beautiful"); Wikipedia gives modern geography (River Gera valley, Thuringian Basin), population (~216,000), and 20th-century political history (Prussia 1802, GDR 1949–1990) that Britannica, written before those events, cannot cover [B:2473:9] [W:9481:1352872890].

**Inference**: The two sources agree on Erfurt's identity and its historic tie to the Electorate of Mainz/Mentz; the apparent disagreement ("capital of Thailand") is an OCR error, not a factual difference. The real drift is coverage: Britannica's entry is a one-sentence gazetteer description, while Wikipedia adds modern geography, demographics, landmarks, and full political history.
